doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Bebop harmony versus the blues
summary: Why bebop changes do not fit the blues and the trade-off between harmonic sophistication and feeling.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: I mean did you feel like you had too much, I don’t know how to put this, too much knowledge from your bebop playing?
That could be it. I felt like I was playing too much because you know, like when you get in the habit of playing like the modern changes, or as you say, bebop, it doesn’t fit with

what they’re doing. You’ve got to think one-three-five, you know what I’m saying? You don’t deviate from that one-three-five or one-four. And you stay in that bag all the time. You can’t play those slick changes like Charlie Parker was playing you know.
I wanted to ask you something.

Do you feel that you have to trade, sometimes trade-off usages of specific parameters. For instance, if you didn’t have all that harmonic sophistication, but you had to endow the music with something, you would do more with the subjective realm — more bending of notes, more blue notes.
In the realm of the blues, yes, I think so. Yeah.
You know you trade-off one thing for the other.
